scene.testo: It is minus 250 degrees Fahrenheit in the shade. On the other side of the same spacecraft, it is plus 250. That is a 500 degree swing, and the astronauts are floating right in the middle of it.

Imagine you are floating inside the International Space Station at 6 AM. Cabin temperature reads about 72 degrees Fahrenheit. You are wearing a T-shirt and shorts. Outside the wall beside your head, the temperature is deadly.
The station circles Earth about 250 miles up at 17,500 mph. It has heaters, yes, but they are not what keeps you alive. The real secret is that space has almost no air to carry the cold to you.

Here is the part that should not make sense. The title of this video says astronauts survive without heaters. But the truth is stranger. Space is not cold the way a freezer is cold. Space is something else entirely.

On Earth, cold bites because air touches your skin and steals heat. Wind makes it worse. Now remove the air. In the vacuum of space, there is almost nothing to touch you, so almost nothing can pull heat away fast.

That means the danger in orbit is not simply freezing. It is a fight between two extremes. Sunlight pours in with no atmosphere to soften it. Shadow sits right next to it. And your spacecraft lives on that border.

Every 90 minutes, the station completes one trip around the planet. That means you see about 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every single day. Each one flips the temperature outside the walls from scorching to freezing and back.

Think about what that means for metal. The outside of the station heats up in sunlight, then cools in darkness, over and over, 16 times a day. Engineers had to design everything to survive that constant stretching and shrinking.

So how do you keep a human comfortable inside a metal box that swings between extremes? You do not fight the heat with heaters. You fight it with a system that moves heat around and throws the extra away.

Start with the surprising fact. The biggest problem on the station is not cold. It is too much heat. Every computer, every light, every laptop, and every astronaut makes warmth, and in a vacuum there is nowhere for it to go.

Your own body gives off roughly 100 watts of heat at rest. That is about the same as an old incandescent light bulb. A crew of six people is like six bulbs burning inside a sealed room that cannot breathe out.

On Earth, a hot room cools itself. Warm air rises, drifts away, and gets replaced. In orbit, there is almost no gravity, so warm air does not rise. It just sits around you in a bubble, wrapping your head like a blanket.

That is why the station has fans running all day and all night. Without them, you could suffocate in your own breath. A pocket of carbon dioxide would gather around your face while you sleep, and fresh air would never reach you.

The same moving air carries heat to the walls and into special cold plates. Water runs through pipes behind those plates, soaking up warmth like a car radiator does for an engine. That water becomes the heart of the cooling system.

Inside the station, the water loop collects heat. Then it passes the heat to a second loop that runs outside, filled with ammonia. Ammonia is toxic, so engineers keep it sealed far away from where you sleep and eat.

That outside ammonia loop travels to huge panels called radiators. They stick out from the station like white wings. Their only job is to glow in infrared light and shed heat into the blackness of space.

Heat leaves a spacecraft in only one way, as radiation. No air, no wind, no water to carry it off. The warmth simply shines away as invisible light. This is how astronauts throw out the heat of their own bodies.

The station has several radiator wings, and each is made of panels. NASA built them to rotate and tilt, turning their edges toward the sun when needed. That keeps them from heating up when they are supposed to be cooling down.

Now picture the outside of the station as a thermos bottle. The walls are covered in layers of thin, shiny material. This is called multilayer insulation, and it looks like crinkled gold or silver foil wrapped around the metal.

Those layers work because a vacuum sits between them. Heat cannot jump across empty space easily, and the shiny surface bounces radiation back. Stack many sheets together, and you get a blanket that stops almost everything.

Now step outside with an astronaut. A spacewalk is where the temperature extremes are real. Sunlit surfaces can reach around 250 degrees Fahrenheit, while shadowed ones drop to roughly minus 250. That is NASA's published range.

The spacesuit is basically a tiny personal spacecraft. It has layers, like the station walls. Inside, a liquid cooling garment hugs the skin, with thin tubes sewn into the fabric that carry cool water across the body.

That is right, a spacesuit has long underwear filled with plumbing. Walking in the sunlight, an astronaut works hard, sweats, and generates heat. The tubes pull that heat away so the person stays comfortable instead of cooking.

Outside the cooling garment, the suit has more layers. There is a pressure bladder that holds air, a restraint layer that keeps the suit from ballooning, and then many thin sheets of insulation under a tough white outer cover.

Why white? Because white reflects sunlight. A dark suit would soak up the sun and overheat in minutes. The bright outer fabric bounces most of the light away, and the layers beneath slow down any heat that sneaks through.

Your fingers are the weak point. Gloves are thin so you can grab tools, yet they touch cold metal handrails. Astronauts have reported that fingers can get uncomfortably cold, and heaters are built into the glove fingertips.

So yes, here is a small honest correction. Some heaters do exist. The station has them, and spacesuit gloves have them. The title is a puzzle, because the main way astronauts stay warm is controlling heat flow, not blasting extra warmth.

Think about a spacewalk lasting six or seven hours. You exit the airlock, and your body temperature must stay steady the entire time. If the cooling water runs too cold, you shiver. Too warm, and you sweat inside a sealed helmet.

Astronauts control this with a dial on the chest of the suit. They can raise or lower the water temperature as they work. It is like adjusting the shower, except the shower is wrapped around your whole body.

Now go back to the shuttle era. Spacecraft like the Space Shuttle used a different trick. The payload bay doors opened in orbit, and radiators on the inside of the doors faced deep space, dumping heat out into the dark.
scene.q: space shuttle payload bay doors open

scene.testo: The shuttle also rolled slowly in orbit sometimes, a technique people called the barbecue roll. Turning like a chicken on a spit spread the sun's heat evenly, so no single side baked while the other side froze.

Now compare this with a house on Earth. In winter, your furnace adds heat. In summer, your air conditioner removes it. A spacecraft is more like a house where the main job is always removing heat, even when the outside is freezing.

Picture the station itself. It is about the length of a football field, roughly 357 feet end to end, including the solar arrays. All of that metal is soaking in sunlight on one side while dark on the other.

Those huge solar panels also run hot. Sunlight hits them, and they turn some of it into electricity. The rest becomes heat. The station tracks the sun with rotating joints to keep the panels pointed just right.
Nearly all the power on board becomes heat in the end. Every watt used by a computer, a light, or a pump turns into warmth inside the walls. That is why moving heat out matters more than making it.

Now think about the old Apollo missions. Spacecraft heading to the Moon needed protection from fierce sunlight. NASA used the passive thermal control roll, slowly rotating the ship about once every few minutes to spread heat evenly.

Apollo crews did report that parts of the cabin got chilly and damp on the way back from the Moon. Water condensed on the walls. Apollo 13 is the famous case, when power was cut and the cabin became very cold.

During Apollo 13, the crew shut down nearly everything to save power. Without equipment making warmth, the cabin cooled to temperatures that NASA records place near the low 40s Fahrenheit. They wore extra clothing and tried to rest.

That shows what happens without active thermal control. Even there, the astronauts survived because the walls were insulated and their bodies still made heat. Being cold in a spacecraft is uncomfortable. Vacuum itself does not instantly freeze you.

Now the most common myth. Movies show an astronaut exposed to vacuum freezing solid in seconds. That is not what physics says. With no air, heat leaves slowly by radiation, so a body would lose warmth far slower than people expect.

The real danger of vacuum is the lack of pressure and oxygen, not instant cold. That is why the suit matters most as a pressure vessel. Warmth is the second job. Air to breathe and pressure to hold your body together come first.

Back inside, the crew keeps the cabin comfortable, around 72 degrees Fahrenheit, which is about 22 degrees Celsius. Astronauts can adjust it a little by module. Some even carry a light jacket, because sitting still near a cool wall can feel chilly.

Sleeping is another small surprise. Astronauts zip into sleeping bags attached to the wall, so they do not drift into equipment. Some say it is warm and cozy inside, since there is no weight and no cold ground below you.

So here is the full answer. Astronauts do not survive space by heating it up. They survive by managing heat. They insulate, reflect sunlight, and use fluid loops to carry warmth to radiators, which release it into the void as light.

And here is the most surprising detail. The hardest job is not staying warm in the dark. It is getting rid of heat in a place where the very thing that kills ordinary heat, the emptiness around you, is also the thing that traps it.

descrizione:
How do astronauts survive the freezing cold of space without heaters? The real answer is stranger than you think. Space is not cold like a freezer, and the biggest danger on the International Space Station is often too much heat, not too little.

In this documentary, we put you inside the station at 6 AM and follow the heat. You will learn how radiators, ammonia loops, cooling garments, and shiny insulation keep astronauts comfortable, why a spacewalk swings between -250°F and +250°F, and what really happened to the Apollo 13 crew when the power went out.

Every fact comes from documented NASA and ESA sources and astronauts' own accounts. Subscribe to Orbital Days for more real stories from life in space.
